t.1.13.1: Śaunaka said: For what reason did that king Janamejaya, a tiger among kings, bring about the end of the snakes by means of the snake sacrifice? Tell me that.
t.1.13.2: And for what reason did Āstīka, the best of the twice-born and foremost of those who recite prayers, set the serpents free from that blazing fire?
t.1.13.3: Whose son was that king who performed the snake sacrifice? And whose son was that foremost of the twice-born? Tell me.
t.1.13.5: Śaunaka said: I wish to hear in full this delightful story of Āstīka, the ancient and illustrious brāhmaṇa.
t.1.13.4: The great Āstīka narrative, in which this is told, O twice-born one, hear all of it from me in full, O best of speakers.
t.1.13.6: The elders dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest call this an ancient history, proclaimed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
t.1.13.7: Formerly, urged by the brāhmaṇas, my father, the sūta Lomaharṣaṇa, the wise disciple of Vyāsa, told this story.
t.1.13.9: The father of Āstīka was a mighty lord, equal to Prajāpati; he was a brahmacārin, restrained in his food, ever devoted to fierce austerity.
t.1.13.8: Having heard it from him, O Śaunaka, I shall now relate to you, since you ask, this tale of Āstīka exactly as it happened.
t.1.13.10: There was a great seer known as Jaratkāru, chaste and celibate, a knower of dharma, foremost among the Yāyāvaras, firm in his vows.
t.1.13.11: Once, while wandering, he saw his own forefathers hanging in a great pit, their feet upward and their faces turned downward.
t.1.13.12: As soon as he saw them, his grandfathers, Jaratkāru said to them: "Who are you, sirs, who hang head-downward in this pit?"
t.1.13.13: We cling to a tuft of vīraṇa grass that has been gnawed away on every side by a hidden rat who dwells permanently in this pit.
t.1.13.14: We are seers called the Yāyāvaras, firm in our vows. Because our line of offspring is dying out, O brahmin, we must sink down into the earth.
t.1.13.15: But our only offspring is the one known as Jaratkāru; ill-fated, he, the son of us of little fortune, has given himself wholly to austerity alone.
t.1.13.16: That deluded one does not wish to take a wife in order to beget sons; because of him, through the destruction of our line, we hang here in this pit.
t.1.13.18: We wish to know, O brahmin, who you are, standing here. And for what purpose do you deign to take pity on us, who are to be pitied?
t.1.13.17: With such a protector we are as protectorless as evildoers are. Who are you, O best of the good, that you grieve for us like a kinsman?
t.1.13.19: You, sirs, are truly my forebears, my fathers together with my grandfathers. Tell me, what shall I do today? I myself am Jaratkāru.
t.1.13.20: Strive diligently, dear son, for the continuation of our lineage, for your own sake and for ours, O mighty one, knowing that this is indeed dharma.
t.1.13.21: For not by the fruits of dharma, dear son, nor by well-amassed austerities do people here attain that state to which those who have sons go.
t.1.13.23: Jaratkāru said: "I will not take a wife; my mind has always been set on this. But for your welfare I will take a wife."
t.1.13.22: Therefore, dear son, at our behest make an effort to take a wife and set your mind on offspring; this is our highest good.
t.1.13.24: And I shall do it in due form under this condition: if I obtain such a one, I will do it, but not otherwise.
t.1.13.26: For who, especially, will give a wife to me, a poor man? Yet I will accept her as alms, if anyone will bestow her.
t.1.13.25: The maiden who will bear the same name as mine and whom her kinsmen wish to give away, that maiden I shall marry according to the ordinance, accepting her as one accepts alms.
t.1.13.27: Thus, O grandfathers, I shall strive for the sake of taking a wife, always according to this rule; I shall not act otherwise.
t.1.13.28: And from that union a being will be born for your deliverance; having reached the eternal abode, let my ancestors rejoice.
t.1.13.29: Then, for the sake of settling down, that brahmin of rigorous vows wandered over the earth seeking a wife, but he did not find a wife.
t.1.13.30: Once that brahmin went into the forest and, remembering the words of his ancestors, cried out three times softly, as it were, seeking the alms of a maiden.
t.1.13.32: For the mind of the great-souled Jaratkāru was set on this: "I shall take as my wife a woman of the same name who is offered to me."
t.1.13.31: Then Vāsuki received him, holding out his sister to him; but he did not accept her, thinking, “She does not bear the same name.”
t.1.13.33: The greatly wise Jaratkāru, of great austerity, said to him: "What is the name of this sister of yours? Tell the truth, O serpent."
t.1.13.34: O Jaratkāru, this Jaratkāru is my sister, my younger sibling, kept long ago for your sake; accept her, O best of the twice-born.
t.1.13.36: To allay that curse, the foremost of serpents gave his sister to that seer, the ascetic of excellent vows.
t.1.13.35: For long ago, O best of those who know brahman, the snakes were cursed by their mother: "At Janamejaya's sacrifice the one whose charioteer is the Wind will burn you."
t.1.13.37: And he accepted her with the rite prescribed by the ordinance, and in her a son named Āstīka was born to that great-souled one.
t.1.13.39: Then, after a long time, the descendant of Pāṇḍu, the lord of men, performed a great sacrifice, the snake sacrifice, so it is heard.
t.1.13.38: He was an ascetic and a great soul, one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, impartial toward the whole world, and the dispeller of the fear of his father's and mother's kin.
t.1.13.40: But when that sacrificial session had begun for the destruction of the serpents, the most illustrious Āstīka released them from that curse.
t.1.13.41: He saved the Nāgas, his maternal uncles, and likewise his other kinsmen, and he saved his ancestors through offspring and through austerity; and by various vows, O brahmin, and by Vedic recitations he became free of debt.
t.1.13.42: He gratified the gods with sacrifices of manifold sacrificial fees, the seers with celibate study, and the forefathers with offspring.
t.1.13.43: Having removed the heavy burden of his ancestors, Jaratkāru, firm in his vows, went to heaven together with his own forefathers.
t.1.13.44: Having obtained a son, Āstīka, and the highest dharma, the sage Jaratkāru went to heaven after a very long time.
t.1.13.45: "This tale of Āstīka has been recounted by me just as it happened. Tell me, O tiger among the Bhṛgus, what more should be narrated?"
